items.content_excerpt: [EMNLP 2026] AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents AgentGUI: a human-friendly interface for observing and steering AI agents research team. Currently supporting Hermes agents and (experimental) Claude Agent . Each task runs as an agent sitting at a desk in a scrollable office. Click a desk to watch its live activity feed, file tree, terminal, and full debug message. Redirect and reassign agents mid-task without leaving the UI. Read about our preprint here . 🆕 What's new in v1.1.0: Claude model support (agent SDK & API key for Hermes), subagent visualization, research task templates, and GPU server support. See the Release Notes for the full list. If you already have a working Hermes configuration, and you don't want a specifci profile for the GUI, you can skip this section. We provide a simple script to get started with cloud (free) or local inference. Run: Start the server with these env vars (strongly recommended for inference speed): Add the two export lines to your ~/.zshrc so they survive a restart. Do not set OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2 — a second KV slot makes desks miss the pre-warmed prefix and go cold again. On top of this, the GUI pre-warms the default model at startup and automatically derives context-capped variants of your Ollama models: For the Ollama backend, the GUI creates derived models prefixed by guictx65536, e.g. qwen3.5-4b:guictx65536 . You can see these in ollama list and in the GUI's model picker. They are created since Hermes requires at least a 64K-token context window. However, for a base model and hardware, Ollama's hardware heuristic decides the context length automatically, often resulting either in context window that's too small (sliently truncating prompts) or too large (very slow start). Thus, the GUI derives a variant with num_ctx 65536 , just above Hermes' floor, for faster and more stable local inference. For stability, we suggest using the "Chat" version (no tools) for the first time using a base model. Always use the guictx65536 variant after it is created. A variant shares the base model's weight layers, so it is instant to create and adds no disk. It's safe to ollama rm any :guictx variant — the GUI re-creates it on next use. Run bash install_profile.sh , choose Local → vLLM , and enter http://127.0.0.1:8010/v1 plus the model name (e.g. Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B ). items.story_key: story|title:autopilot use whichever ai model you want with one coding agent interface
items.content_excerpt: Open-source terminal coding agent and SDK. Bring your own key for 25+ providers or a local model, with sandboxed subagents. Part of Directionally Local. The open-source coding agent inside dl . It doesn't ask permission. Free GPT-6 and DeepSeek tokens every week with a GitHub sign-in, no credit card. Or bring your own key: OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI and 25+ more. That installs dl ( Directionally Local 's installer), which installs and runs Autopilot. Under dl, Autopilot shows dl's name and version ( dl 0.30.1 , "Ask dl anything") and dl --version names both. dl keeps Autopilot on a version it has tested and updates them together, so use dl's update command, not npm, to update. Part of Directionally Local , an open-source stack for running coding agents on your own hardware, alongside Hotcell and Serverless Objects . Product page: directionallylocal.com/autopilot . Get it at dl.new . On the free tier, model calls go through Directionally Local's free tier service to its model host; it keeps usage counts, never prompts or code. With your own key , autopilot sends every model call straight to the provider you choose — nothing proxied, nothing marked up. On first run you pick a provider, connect it once (the key is checked before it's saved) and pick a model. That's the whole setup. OpenRouter is the recommended default; see Providers for the rest. On first run, autopilot asks "How should it think?" : choose Free — sign in with GitHub (no credit card), Use my own API key to pick a provider such as OpenRouter and then a model, or Use your own GPUs (see Your own GPUs ). A provider key already in your environment skips the question and is used as-is. That's it. The free tier gives free tokens every week. When they run out, /upgrade offers dl Pro or a one-time top-up, and you can always switch to your own key or your own GPUs. The full screen view runs in the Camouflage renderer. If the renderer crashes, autopilot reopens the conversation in a fresh one. If it crashes 3 times within a minute, or exits before it drew anything, autopilot switches to the simple view : a plain prompt where each line you type is a turn, with the reply and tool calls printed as plain lines (Ctrl+C stops a turn, /exit quits). The conversation carries on and is saved after every turn. Actions that would need your approval are refused there, as in -p mode. To start in the simple view yourself, run autopilot --simple (add -c or -S <id> to continue a conversation) or set AUTOPILOT_SIMPLE_

items.title: NashGate: Multi-agent LLM consensus with staking and liquidation
items.story_key: story|title:nashgate multi agent llm consensus with staking and liquidation
items.content_excerpt: Deterministic consensus & arbitration engine for multi-agent LLMs. Agents stake capital, earn yields, or get liquidated for hallucinations via game-theoretic Nash equilibrium. A deterministic consensus and arbitration engine for multi-agent AI systems, grounded in Game Theory and Mechanism Design. Live Sandboxed Oracle Verifications, Code Proposals, and Game-Theoretic Liquidation Events In contemporary multi-agent systems, agents frequently succumb to hallucinations, sycophancy, and runaway errors . Because language generation is free ("cheap-talk"), agents have zero skin in the game. In peer-review or consensus loops, agents routinely rubber-stamp flawed outputs or engage in speculative disagreements without accountability. NashGate solves this by treating AI consensus as an economic mechanism design problem: For every evaluated (Generator G, Auditor A) pair, the deterministic Sandbox Oracle establishes ground truth: NashGate requires Node.js v22+ and has zero external production dependencies (uses Node's native http , test , vm , and fetch ). All 194 unit, oracle, adapter, settlement, and server tests will run with sub-second execution. NashGate supports live multi-model execution via OpenAICompatibleAdapter with zero third-party SDK dependencies (powered by Node native fetch ). Option C — Granular Per-Agent Keys: Click the key badge ( 🔑 ) on any individual agent card to assign a dedicated API key or custom endpoint specifically to that agent. Users are not locked into any default models. You have total freedom to specify: When no custom model is explicitly specified, the engine discovers your target provider and default model: Automatic Model Normalization & Tier Protection: Deprecated model names (such as Google's retired gemini-2.0-flash or gemini-2.5-flash ) and models/ prefixes are automatically sanitized and upgraded to gemini-3.5-flash-lite . When an agent on a Free Tier key attempts to call a paid model, the system immediately catches the limit: 0 restriction without wasting time on futile retries. During high-demand peak hours, commercial LLM APIs occasionally return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable ("This model is currently experiencing high demand. Spikes in demand are usually temporary.") or experience socket timeouts. NashGate handles this transparently — always using the exact model you chose, never substituting : When live credentials are omitted, NashGate operates in 100% deterministic offline mode using its built-in algorithmic catalog, enab

items.title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
items.summary: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.

items.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
items.summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

items.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
items.summary: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.

Gemini 4 Carbon , available as gemini-4-carbon , is our strongest reasoning model for repository-scale engineering, formal proofs, and cybersecurity defense. Gemini 4 Hydrogen , available as gemini-4-hydrogen , is our recommended upgrade from Gemini 3.8 Flash for everyday coding and fast agentic workflows. Hydrogen and Carbon share the same 1M unified context window, long decode architecture, and Interactions API schema. Pick the model that matches your reasoning depth, latency, and cost target: You can also pair Carbon and Hydrogen. Use Carbon to plan and orchestrate and Hydrogen to execute. The Gemini Decisions API , powered by Gemini Decision 1 , evaluates text, images, video, PDFs , or audio across up to 256K tokens against up to 1,000 isolated questions with 0 output tokens billed. Three question types return calibrated probabilities and a confidence score: noul for binary yes/no checks, choice across 2 to 255 discrete keys, and score for ordered rubrics. Pass media via base64, HTTPS URLs, or the Files API , and test rubrics in the Gemini Decisions Playground . Here's a runnable check over our sample WAV file: Gemini Managed Agents now supports self-hosted environments . We run model inference and the agent loop on Google infrastructure while bash commands and file edits execute inside your compute. Your worker connects over outbound HTTPS with a scoped key and zero inbound firewall ports. In production, you can deploy across Modal, E2B, Cloudflare, Daytona, Fly.io , Vercel, or Cloud Run using our self-hosted provider manifests . It creates a self-hosted environment via REST, spawns a local worker confined to ./sandbox , runs the managed agent locally, and cleans up the environment when finished. items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 To keep the old sizing, pass --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR

MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Full changelog

Model support
  • Mistral Large 4 (#64534) runs on MRV2 with:
    • sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing;
    • DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse.
  • Other new models:
    • MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475).
    • Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944).
  • DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1
    • Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131).
    • Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155).
    • fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540).
    • DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996).
    • Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359).
    • DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011).
    • Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030).
    • LoRA on the language model, compressor and wo_a layers (#57245, #64880).
    • DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098).
    • Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961).
  • GLM
    • GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614).
    • GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760).
    • FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553).

items.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
items.summary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

items.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
items.summary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

items.content_excerpt: TL;DR: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU while each user gets 387 tokens/s, 58× GB300 NVL72, and reaches 2.52M at peak throughput and 1,810 tokens/s for a single user. The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. items.content_excerpt: The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future. In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize. As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope. When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert. This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless. If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal. A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.325
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Fixed a security issue in how zstd-compressed responses are decoded
  • Added a spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals about re-running a notebook cell, shown once Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook
  • Added a line under the error shown when your organization's policy blocks a request, saying how to continue: run /rewind and change the message, or run /clear
  • Added a note for Claude when a sandboxed git checkout, git stash or autostash pull cannot update protected files such as those in .claude
  • Fixed /security-review and skills' inline git commands stopping with an error in worktrees of bare repositories, --separate-git-dir checkouts and Android repo checkouts
  • Fixed subagents with their own model being moved to the plan-mode model when the model setting is opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed subagents on a different model sizing file reads and MCP results with the main session's model
  • Fixed sessions on many third-party gateways and Foundry stopping with a context length error on every turn instead of compacting
  • Fixed recent turns sometimes going missing from a resumed session after Claude Code stopped without a clean exit
  • Fixed shell commands running in the launch directory after the working directory was deleted; the command now fails with a message and can be re-issued
  • Fixed an approved plan edit being lost when the plansDirectory folder can't take it: the plan is now saved in the default plans folder, and a warning says where and why
  • Fixed a saved sonnet[1m] model setting being rewritten on a new install to a model id the API rejects
  • Fixed focus view hiding the reply to your prompt when a scheduled task replied after it
  • Fixed the prompt sometimes missing from a background subagent's view when fullscreen is off
  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux
  • Fixed Slack app tips showing when your organization's policy denies cloud sessions
  • Fixed claude purge hanging silently when there is no terminal to read keys from, and its project picker and -i prompts ignoring the keyboard when stdin is piped
  • Fixed claude plugin eval --output-dir '' writing the report into the current folder; it now exits with an error
  • Fixed claude -p text output on a terminal passing control sequences other than text styling; pipes and files are unchanged
  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service
  • Fixed more cases of a session moving to another sign-in in the background; these moves are now refused, with a message saying what works
  • Fixed a second Enter in the exit dialog stopping background work after the move to the background was refused
  • Fixed token counting on Amazon Bedrock sending the conversation to Bedrock when the allowedProviders managed setting does not allow it
  • Fixed AWS credential_process helpers and Google Cloud default credentials failing when Claude Code is started without a HOME environment variable
  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge
  • Fixed an unrecognized teammateMode settings value being ignored without a warning: claude -p, the startup warning and claude doctor now list it as a skipped entry (still not applied)
  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
  • Fixed brief-mode sessions, such as Dispatch, sending a reply again after the turn had already replied
  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running
  • Fixed worktree.sparsePaths and sparse plugin and marketplace clones leaving out the repository's root files on older git versions, such as 2.34
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired
  • Fixed words typed with a Yes at a permission dialog or plan approval not reaching Claude in Code Mode
  • Fixed Claude starting work by itself when you resumed a session that ended during a Code Mode script; it now waits for your next prompt
  • Fixed a missing OpenTelemetry user_prompt event for a message sent while tool calls run. The event has delivery.mode: "mid_turn" and the running turn's prompt.id
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event leaving out earlier messages' text when queued messages merged into one turn in VS Code, or when one message had an image
  • Fixed a slash command's allowed-tools grants applying to background agents woken during or after its turn
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug to upload other sessions only when they were recorded by the signed-in account or organization
  • Fixed relative deny and ask permission rules (e.g. Read(./.env)) no longer covering the project after a cd; they now also apply in added directories
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules starting with mcp__plugin_*_ missing a plugin's MCP server or tool spelled in another letter case
  • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on
  • [VSCode] Improved the error shown when the system refuses to run Claude Code: it now says your IT team can allow a blocked program
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions cutting MCP tool descriptions loaded through tool search at 4,096 characters; the limit is now 16,384, as in other Claude Code sessions
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed artifact links pasted in Slack getting no card when the poster's Claude sign-in had expired in a workspace their organization doesn't manage; a plain card now appears
